newsitem.title: INDIA: India extends Sobhraj's detention by two weeks.
newsitem.headline: India extends Sobhraj's detention by two weeks.

text.p: Notorious criminal Charles Sobhraj was on Monday ordered held in detention for two more weeks by the Indian government following a delay in his deportation to France.
"...the FRRO had restricted his movement till yesterday but now they have extended that by another two weeks," Sobhraj's lawyer Rajan Bakshi told Reuters by telephone.
The Foreigners' Regional Registration Officer (FRRO) had passed an order on February 17 restricting Sobhraj's movement in India until March 2.

Last week India ordered the deportation of Sobhraj to France, as he is presumed to be a French citizen, and barred him from re-entering the country again, saying his presence was prejudicial to the nation's security.
"Since the last order was only for two weeks and lapsed on Sunday, the FRRO passed a fresh order," Bakshi said.
Bakshi said the order would be effective till March 17 or until the time Sobhraj left India, whichever date was earlier.
Sobhraj's expulsion from India has been delayed while French authorities study his past record and nationality claims before issuing him the travel documents.
Born to an Indian father and a Vietnamese mother, Sobhraj claims that he is a French citizen.

Sobhraj was first arrested in India for holding up a hotel jewellery shop in 1971. He has since been charged with a long string of crimes including murder, serving time for some and winning acquittal in others.
India convicted Sobhraj in 1978 of murdering a French tourist. He was acquitted 20 months later on appeal, but remained in New Delhi's Tihar jail on lesser charges.
Another judge sentenced Sobhraj to life imprisonment in 1982 for poisoning an Israeli tourist, but again he was acquitted on appeal.
In 1986, Sobhraj escaped while being held pending an extradition request from Thailand to face charges of murder and attempted murder. He was recaptured 24 days later.
Thailand's 20-year statute of limitations later expired and Thai police said late last year that Sobhraj no longer could be tried on their charges.
Police in Hong Kong said last month they still wanted to interview Sobhraj about drugging and robbery cases in the British colony in the 1970s.
A FRRO official said Sobhraj would be set free once he was in France.
